newsitem.title: UK: B.A.T extend losses after U.S. tobacco deal.
newsitem.headline: B.A.T extend losses after U.S. tobacco deal.

text.p: Shares in B.A.T Industries Plc dropped on Monday after the company said it expected its Brown & Williamson unit to make an initial payment of around $1.7 billion under a landmark U.S. tobacco settlement.
The shares were 24p weaker at 565 by 1130 GMT.

Analysts said the agreement between U.S. states and the industry announced on Friday was reasonably positive for the company, but its shares were hit by profit-taking after gaining ground in anticipation of the deal.
Under the agreement, tobacco companies will pay $368.5 billion over 25 years in compensation for the cost of treating smoking-related illnesses in return for immunity from further litigation.
"The deal was a fairly good one for B.A.T but the shares had a good run ahead of the news," one dealer said. "People bought on the rumour and sold on the fact."
Analysts said tobacco shares, which have been dogged by the threat of escalating legal claims, will eventually show relief.
"Sometimes it's just better to travel than to arrive," said Simon Willis, industry analyst at Charterhouse Tilney.

"Tobacco shares have been quite buoyant over the last few weeks and we have to bear in mind that this proposed deal still has to go through Congress," Willis said. "The companies have got the best deal they can get and if the deal is altered at all in this process, it can only get worse."
Willis still expects the share price to climb through the six pounds level.
"We could see the shares trade up to 630p on a successful deal and the prospect of a demerger is the icing on the cake."
The Financial Times Lex column was also positive about the prospects for B.A.T after the settlement.
"B.A.T Industries could be the biggest winner," the newspaper said.

"It has a comparatively small U.S. tobacco business which is strongest in discount brands. Assume a 20-percent drop in U.S. profits and subtract B.A.T's 720 million stg after-tax down payment and its U.S. business would still be worth well over two billion stg," it said.
"That's definitely better than the current implied valuation of next to nothing."
Analysts expect B.A.T to turn its attention now to a demerger of its tobacco and insurance businesses in an effort to boost shareholder value.
"But I think a demerger was much more likely when the share price was nearer five pounds than six," Willis said.
B.A.T's Brown & Williamson is the third largest cigarette-maker in the U.S., with brands such as Kent and Lucky Strike.
Shares in Britain's Imperial Tobacco and Gallaher Group, which do not have the same exposure to U.S. litigation, were also sharply lower on Monday.
Imperial fell 13-1/2p to 393-1/2p and shares in Gallaher, Britain's largest cigarette maker, were 9-1/2p lower at 290-1/2.
